title: Nobody Gave Mimoh Chakraborty a Chance. He Just Beat Diljit, Kangana, and Manoj Bajpayee on Opening Day.
excerpt: Haunted 3D: Echoes of the Past opened at ₹2.72 crore on Friday, winning a brutal four-way box office clash that everyone expected to go very differently.
body:
Let's talk about what was supposed to happen on Friday.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=0lMGLjj6CeE

Diljit Dosanjh was opening in an Imtiaz Ali period romance about Partition, with A.R. Rahman on the soundtrack and Naseeruddin Shah lending gravitas. Kangana Ranaut was playing the nurse who stared down Kasab during the 26/11 attacks. Manoj Bajpayee was headlining a financial thriller about the week India nearly defaulted on its sovereign debt. Three serious films by serious people with serious box-office expectations.

And then Mimoh Chakraborty walked in.

Haunted 3D: Echoes of the Past — a horror sequel fifteen years in the making, directed by Vikram Bhatt, with production values that critics politely described as "B-movie level" — opened on Friday at ₹2.72 crore across 2,907 shows. That number might not sound massive. But consider the context: it was more than double Kangana's Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata (₹1.00 crore), comfortably ahead of Imtiaz Ali's Main Vaapas Aaunga (₹1.28 crore), and nearly three times what Manoj Bajpayee's Governor managed (₹0.94 crore).

The biggest star in a four-way Friday clash was a ghost.

To understand why this matters, you have to go back to 2011. The original Haunted 3D was a genuine hit — the highest-opening Indian horror film at the time, grossing ₹35 crore worldwide on a shoestring budget. But the brand of supernatural horror that Vikram Bhatt built through the Raaz and 1920 franchises had, in recent years, felt like a relic. The genre moved toward comedy-horror — see Bhooth Bangla's spectacular ₹269 crore run. The assumption was that earnest, atmospheric horror was dead at the box office.

Friday suggests it was just sleeping.

The occupancy numbers tell their own story. While the national average sat at around 15% across nearly 3,000 shows, Lucknow hit a staggering 50%. Mumbai clocked 37.8%. Kolkata registered 33.8%, NCR came in at 32.8%, and Bhopal reported 38.3%. The pattern is unmistakable: Tier 2 and Tier 3 India showed up in force. Smaller centres across UP, Bihar, and Rajasthan reported occupancy in the 30-50% range — numbers that would make most mid-budget openers envious. Night shows were consistently the strongest, with Mumbai touching 56% after dark.

Reviews, it should be noted, have not been kind. India Today gave 2.5 stars out of 5, noting "weak VFX and minimal scares." Bollywood Hungama was blunter at 2 stars: "a promising story that suffers due to a poor climax and the excessive, tacky use of VFX and AI." The Times of India gave 2 stars, calling it "a horror sequel haunted by its inability to move beyond the formulas of the past." And Rediff went scorched earth with 1 star, writing that the film had "no real scares, no real acting, no real sets."

None of that mattered to Friday's audience.

What this opening reveals is something the industry keeps learning and forgetting in cycles: there is an audience — largely in heartland India, largely young, largely male — that will always show up for accessible, unpretentious horror entertainment. They don't check IMDb ratings. They don't read Firstpost reviews. They want a darkened theatre, a jump scare, and the specific thrill of watching something terrifying in 3D with their friends on a Friday night. Haunted 3D delivered exactly that promise, and nothing more was required.

For NRI audiences tracking from abroad, the real story isn't the Haunted numbers — it's the drought they exposed. This has been Bollywood's driest stretch since Bhooth Bangla opened in April. Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai has been the only film showing any sustained legs, and even that is modest by blockbuster standards. None of Friday's four releases are tracking toward breakout territory. The real question is whether anything can build momentum before Cocktail 2 arrives on June 19 and Welcome to the Jungle follows on June 26. Until then, the summer window's opening salvo belongs to the sequel nobody expected to fire.

Trade analysts are now projecting an ₹8 crore opening weekend for Haunted 3D if Saturday and Sunday hold. Not earth-shattering. But for a film that cost a fraction of its competitors, with a lead whose last major release barely registered, in a slot nobody expected him to win — it's the kind of story that keeps Bollywood interesting.

Vikram Bhatt once said horror is the great equalizer of Indian cinema. On Friday, at 2,907 screens across the country, he proved it.
